newsitem.title: UK: Asian names line up to borrow in Eurobond market.
newsitem.headline: Asian names line up to borrow in Eurobond market.

text.p: Asian credits will figure strongly in the international bond markets in coming months, with sovereigns and supranationals having raised most their funds for the year, dealers said on Monday.
"A lot of supply will be coming out of Asia (in the next few months)," said a syndicate manager at a U.S. bank. "There is a marked absence of European names in the pipeline at the moment."
Today, the Export-Import Bank of Korea issued a $500 million five-year Eurobond. Dealers said Korea Development Bank was looking to follow in the near term with a similar issue.

"The last quarter of the year is traditionally the time when (sovereign and supranational) borrowers do their catching up, but no one is massively behind in their funding," said an origination official at a U.S. bank.
The lack of supranational and European sovereign supply, which traditionally feeds the institutional market's desire for large, liquid Eurobonds, can be explained by two factors, dealers said.
"There has been a strong trend for frequent borrowers to raise money through retail-targeted, arbitrage-driven deals," a trader at a Japanese bank said.
He said many borrowers had pre-funded and were in no hurry to borrow funds.
"This has provided them with lower borrowing costs, and demand from retail will continue strong as redemptions pick up in the next few months," he said.
Among Asian borrowers, Japanese credits are also forming a long queue.
JR East is considering a $500 million 10-year bond. City of Yokohama plans a $300 million 10-year deal and Metropolis of Tokyo is eyeing a similar deal.
Lower down the credit spectrum, Malaysian oil company Petronas is said to be close to awarding a mandate for a $500 million Eurobond.
A syndicate manager at a U.S. bank said big European borrowers might decide to take a more strategic approach for their last requirements than they have been so far this year.
"Arbitrage has provided cheaper funds, but the deals become illiquid very quickly, and it does nothing for borrowers in terms of expanding their investor basis," he said.
"Some borrowers, because they have been so focused on opportunistic borrowing, may do more strategic deals and try and push the boundaries of the markets a bit," he said.
As an example, the syndicate manager cited Suedwestdeutsche Landesbank, on a roadshow for a $500 million five-year bond.
"They want to establish their name with Asian investors, and need to do a strategic deal as a result," he said.
Dollar issuance is likely to dominate the Eurobond market in the coming months, but increased investor appetite for marks has also been noted.
"Five- and 10-year dollars will see a lot of activity, and five-, seven- and 10-year marks too," said a syndicate manager at a U.S. bank.
"Marks have been quiet lately with a lot of investors wary about the market. (But) the outlook is now a bit more bullish, so we expect more mark buying from institutions," he said.
But despite a shortage of suitable investments, institutions in particular remain very choosy, dealers said.
"In theory, demand for five-year dollars, for example, is very strong," said a trader at a U.S. bank.
"But the pricing has to be absolutely right. Institutions will not buy something they do not see as good value, and if this happens, a deal is dead in the water," he said.
-- Aline van Duyn, London Newsroom +44 171 542 7748
